title: The Cell and the Cell Theory
summary: The cell as the basic unit of life, single-celled and many-celled organisms, and the three ideas of the cell theory.

p: The cell is the smallest unit of structure and function of living things. It is the 'building block' of life. Some organisms, such as amoeba and bacteria, are made of just one cell (unicellular). Others, such as humans, are made of trillions of cells (multicellular).

The cell theory was developed by Matthias Schleiden, Theodor Schwann and Rudolf Virchow. It has three main ideas: 1. All living things are made of one or more cells. 2. The cell is the basic unit of structure and function in living things. 3. All new cells come from cells that already exist (by cell division).
Most cells are far too small to see with the naked eye. We need a microscope to see them. The first person to see and name cells was Robert Hooke in 1665, when he looked at thin slices of cork.

In a many-celled organism, cells have different shapes for their jobs. Red blood cells are small and round to carry oxygen. Nerve cells are long to carry messages. Muscle cells can shorten to cause movement. Root hair cells have thin extensions to take in water.

title: Plant Cells and Animal Cells Compared, and Using a Microscope
summary: Five differences between plant and animal cells, and how to use a light microscope to see onion and cheek cells.

p: Study the table.

sections.h: Why do plants have these extras?
p: Plants stand still and make their own food, so they need a rigid cell wall for support, chloroplasts for photosynthesis and a big vacuole of water to keep the cells firm (turgid). Animals move about and eat food, so they need flexible cells and no chloroplasts.

A microscope lets us see objects too small for the naked eye. Eyepiece: the lens you look through. Objective lenses: the lenses that magnify the specimen. Stage: the platform that holds the slide. Coarse and fine focus knobs: make the picture sharp. Light source: a mirror or lamp. The total magnification is the eyepiece magnification multiplied by the objective magnification, for example 10 × 40 = 400 times.

Onion cells: peel a thin layer from the inside of an onion scale, place it on a slide with a drop of water or iodine stain, lower a cover slip gently and look. You will see rectangular cells with cell walls and nuclei. Cheek cells: gently scrape the inside of your cheek with a clean cotton bud, smear it on a slide with a drop of stain, and you will see irregular cells with nuclei but no cell walls. Always start with the lowest-power lens and use the coarse focus first.

title: Levels of Organisation and Tissues
summary: From cell to organism, the school analogy, and the main animal and plant tissues.

p: In many-celled organisms the body is built up in levels. Level 1, cells: the basic unit (muscle cell, nerve cell, skin cell). Level 2, tissues: a group of similar cells doing one job. Level 3, organs: different tissues working together to do a big job. Level 4, organ systems: several organs working together for a main life process. Level 5, the organism: the whole living thing (a human, a dog, a tree).

img.alt: A pyramid from atoms and molecules at the top, through cells, tissues, organs and organ systems down to the whole organism
img.cap: Levels of organisation, from small to large.

p: A cell is like one student. A tissue is like a class of students doing the same kind of work. An organ is like a department (with students and teachers who have different jobs). An organ system is like the whole school. The organism is the whole education system working as one.
Study the table.

head: Tissue
Function
Examples
rows: Skin, lining of the mouth and stomach
Contracts and relaxes to cause movement

p: Meristematic tissue: at the tips of roots and shoots; cells divide to give growth. Dermal tissue: the outer 'skin' (epidermis) that protects the plant. Vascular tissue: the transport system. Xylem carries water and minerals up from the roots. Phloem carries food (sugars) made in the leaves to all other parts of the plant, both up and down. (The lesson note says phloem carries food 'down'; it carries it to wherever it is needed.) Ground tissue: fills the space between the others and includes the cells that do photosynthesis.

title: Organs, Organ Systems and Coordination
summary: Examples of organs and the main human organ systems, and how they work together.

p: An organ is made of several tissues working together. The stomach, for example, has muscle tissue to churn food, epithelial tissue to line it and nervous tissue to control it. Other organs: heart, lungs, brain, kidney, and, in plants, the leaf, stem and root.
Study the table.

head: System
Organs
Function
rows: Mouth, stomach, small and large intestine, liver
Carries oxygen and nutrients round the body
Takes in oxygen and removes carbon dioxide

p: The systems must work together, or coordinate, to keep us alive. When you run, your muscles (muscular system) need more oxygen. Your lungs (respiratory system) work faster to take it in and your heart (circulatory system) pumps faster to carry it to the muscles. The brain (nervous system) controls all this. If one system fails, the others are affected.

title: Heredity: Genes, Inherited and Acquired Traits
summary: What heredity and genetics are, how genes pass traits, and the difference between inherited and acquired traits.

p: Heredity is the passing of traits (characteristics) from parents to their children. It is why children look like their parents. Genetics is the science that studies heredity.

Genes are the units of heredity: short pieces of DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) on the chromosomes in the nucleus of our cells. Genes are like an instruction manual that decides our traits. A human cell has 46 chromosomes, 23 from each parent.

img.alt: Human chromosomes with a man and a woman and arrows pointing to a child, showing that traits come from both parents
img.cap: A child receives half of its chromosomes from each parent.

p: These are features you are born with, passed on through genes. You cannot choose them. Examples: blood group (A, B, AB, O), skin colour, eye colour, natural hair colour and texture, and the shape of your face.

These are features you get during your life. They are not in your genes and cannot be passed on to your children. Examples: scars, muscles from exercise, speaking English or Yoruba, knowledge from school, a tattoo, tribal marks, and bleached skin.
Is the ability to speak French inherited or acquired? Acquired, because a child born to French speakers who is brought up elsewhere will not speak French unless taught.

title: Variation and Simple Genetic Inheritance
summary: Why individuals differ, why variation helps species survive, and how dominant and recessive genes work with a Punnett square.

p: Variation means the differences in traits among individuals of the same species. This is why people in your class (except identical twins) look different. Causes: sexual reproduction mixes genes from two parents to give new combinations; mutations (changes in genes) give new traits; and the environment can change how traits show, for example two plants with the same genes grow to different heights if one gets more sunlight.

img.alt: A diagram of four related ideas: variation, heredity, genes and inheritance
img.cap: Genetics: variation, heredity, genes and inheritance.

p: Variation is the raw material for adaptation and evolution. It lets a species survive when the environment changes. Example: in a flock of goats, some have thick fur and some thin. If the weather turns very cold, the thin-furred ones may die while the thick-furred ones live, breed and pass on the thick-fur gene.

For each trait you have two genes, one from each parent. A dominant gene shows its trait whenever it is present, and is written with a capital letter (T for tall). A recessive gene shows its trait only when there is no dominant gene, and is written with a small letter (t for short). Dominant does not mean 'stronger' or 'more common'; it only means that it shows up when both are present.
Tall plant: TT or Tt. Short plant: tt only.
The father has free earlobes (Ee, with E dominant) and the mother has attached earlobes (ee). Each parent passes on one gene. The Punnett square shows the possible children.

Two of the four boxes are ee, so there is a 50% chance that a child has attached earlobes. (Ear-lobe shape is used in schools as a simple example; in reality it is not controlled by a single gene, so real families may not follow this pattern exactly.)

title: Adaptation: Habitat and Structural Adaptations
summary: What adaptation is, why it matters, and how animals and plants are built for their habitats, including the camel, fish, cactus, polar bear and Galapagos finches.

p: A habitat is the natural home of an organism, such as the desert, a river or a forest. An adaptation is a special feature or behaviour that helps an organism survive and reproduce in its habitat. Well-adapted organisms find food, escape enemies and have young; poorly adapted ones die out.
Study the table.

head: Organism
Habitat

rows: Hump stores fat, which can be broken down for energy (and gives some water); long eyelashes keep out sand; wide flat feet stop it sinking in the sand
Gills take in oxygen dissolved in water; fins and a streamlined body for fast swimming; scales for protection
Spines instead of leaves cut water loss and keep animals away; thick fleshy stem stores water
Thick fur and blubber (fat) for warmth; white-looking fur helps it hide

p: Many people think the camel's hump stores water. It stores fat. When the fat is used up in the body, it gives energy, and some water is made as a by-product.

The picture shows the finches that Charles Darwin studied on the Galapagos Islands. Their beaks differ in shape and size depending on what they eat: large strong beaks for cracking seeds, thin pointed beaks for catching insects, and so on. This is a structural adaptation to food.

title: Behavioural and Functional Adaptations, and Why Adaptation Matters
summary: Actions and body processes that help survival, such as migration, hibernation, venom and colour change, and why adaptation is vital.

p: These are actions an organism takes to survive. Migration: many birds travel long distances to find food or a warmer place (some European birds spend our dry season in Nigeria). Hibernation: some animals, such as bears, sleep through the winter to save energy when food is scarce. Nocturnal activity: owls, rats and bats rest in the hot day and come out at night. Living in groups: lions hunt as a pride, and meerkats post a lookout.

These are internal body processes or chemicals. Poison or venom: snakes make venom to kill prey, and some plants make poison against plant-eaters. Colour change: a chameleon changes its skin colour. It does this mainly to communicate with other chameleons and to control its body temperature, and sometimes to blend in with its surroundings. (The lesson note gives camouflage as the main purpose.) Other examples: sweating to cool the body and a thick layer of mucus on fish to protect from germs.
Study the table.

Adaptation lets a species survive and keep reproducing in its habitat. When the environment changes faster than a species can adapt, the species may die out (become extinct). This is why protecting habitats is important.
